evidence: Vicipaedia, the discussion page of its article Intellegentia artificialis
Quint. 5.1.1: probātiōnēs artificiālēs, proofs made by the art (Lewis & Short s.v. artificiālis)
terms.comment: The name in current Latin use, matching the modern languages; Vicipaedia’s article is so titled, which is weak evidence by itself. artificiālis is Quintilian’s word for what is made by the rules of an art, as against what is given. Chosen over Cicero’s artificiōsus (next) because that word also means skilful, so that intellegentia artificiōsa could be heard as “skilful intelligence”. In talk the thing one speaks to is plainly māchina (see AI, a system one talks to).

terms.gloss: intelligence made by art, not by nature
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.72: ea genera dīvīnandī nōn nātūrālia, sed artificiōsa dīcuntur (Lewis & Short s.v. artificiōsus)
M-O s.v. artificial, man-made: artificiosus, a, um (Egger)
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for what comes from art as opposed to nature, and Egger’s for things man-made (an artificial leg, an artificial satellite). Its first sense is skilful, accomplished (Lewis & Short).

ai-name.html: On Vicipaedia’s discussion page (2009–2015) the editors weighed artificiōsus, which the classical dictionaries give for “artificial”, against artificiālis, defended as a Neo-Latin term needed for a modern idea; prūdentia artis and intellegentia arte facta were also put forward. A report of the article quotes its first line as Intellegentia artificialis, vel intellegentia ficticia, est subdisciplina informatica. Morgan–Owens lists “artificial intelligence” under “artificial, man-made” without giving Latin for it.

phrases.latin: Num māchina vērē intellegit? Id etiam doctī ambigunt.
phrases.english: Does the machine really understand? Even learned people argue about that.
